questions.question: What are the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming in Java, and can you give a real example of each?
questions.title: Four Pillars of OOP in Java
questions.direct_answer: The four pillars are Encapsulation (hiding internal state behind methods), Inheritance (child classes reuse parent behavior), Polymorphism (one interface, multiple implementations — like calling animal.speak() and getting different sounds), and Abstraction (exposing only what matters, hiding complexity). In real Java code: encapsulation is private fields + public getters, inheritance is extends, polymorphism is method overriding + interface implementations, abstraction is abstract classes and interfaces.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can explain OOP with concrete Java examples — not textbook definitions. They want to hear you think in objects, not memorize acronyms.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reciting definitions without examples, or confusing abstraction with encapsulation — they overlap but serve different purposes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real-world analogy alongside Java code. Show you've applied OOP in a project, not just studied it.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Encapsulation protects invariants** — `private` fields with public methods enforce business rules like 'balance cannot go negative'
- **Inheritance enables code reuse** — `extends` lets child classes inherit behavior, but creates tight coupling; prefer composition for non-hierarchical relationships
- **Polymorphism decouples callers from implementations** — `processAccount(BankAccount a)` works with any subclass; behavior changes without changing the calling code
- **Abstraction hides complexity** — interfaces and abstract classes expose the 'what' and hide the 'how', enabling swappable implementations
- **Two forms of polymorphism** — compile-time (method overloading, same name different params) and runtime (method overriding via inheritance/interfaces)

Object-Oriented Programming in Java rests on four pillars, and the best way to remember them is through a real scenario — imagine you're building a banking application.

**Encapsulation** is about protecting data. Your `BankAccount` class has a `private double balance` field. Nobody outside the class can set it directly — they must call `deposit()` or `withdraw()`, which enforce business rules like 'balance cannot go negative'. The data and the rules that protect it live together inside the class.

**Inheritance** lets you reuse behavior. A `SavingsAccount extends BankAccount` — it automatically gets deposit/withdraw methods but adds `calculateInterest()`. You don't copy-paste code; the child inherits from the parent.

**Polymorphism** means one interface, many forms. If you have a method `processAccount(BankAccount account)`, you can pass a `SavingsAccount`, `CheckingAccount`, or `BusinessAccount` — the method doesn't care. Each subclass can override `calculateFees()` differently. The calling code stays the same; the behavior changes based on the actual object type.

**Abstraction** hides complexity. Your `PaymentGateway` interface exposes `processPayment(amount)`. The caller doesn't know if it's using Stripe, PayPal, or a bank API internally. You've abstracted away the 'how' and exposed only the 'what'.

- Encapsulation is not just 'make fields private' — it's grouping data with the behavior that operates on it, enforcing invariants
- Inheritance creates tight coupling — prefer composition ('has-a') over inheritance ('is-a') when the relationship isn't truly hierarchical
- Polymorphism has two forms in Java: compile-time (method overloading) and runtime (method overriding via inheritance/interfaces)
- Abstraction and Encapsulation overlap — abstraction is the design decision (what to expose), encapsulation is the implementation mechanism (how to hide)

Design a simple `Shape` hierarchy with `Circle` and `Rectangle`. Use all four pillars: encapsulate dimensions, inherit from a base class, make `calculateArea()` polymorphic, and abstract the shape concept with an interface or abstract class. Write the Java code.

followup_questions: What's the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
When would you choose composition over inheritance?
What is the diamond problem and how does Java solve it with interfaces?

questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() in Java? When would you use each?
questions.title: == vs .equals() in Java
questions.direct_answer: == compares references (do both variables point to the exact same object in memory?). .equals() compares content (do the two objects have the same meaningful value?). For primitives, use ==. For objects like String, always use .equals(). The classic trap: new String("hello") == new String("hello") is false (different objects), but new String("hello").equals(new String("hello")) is true (same content).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand reference vs value equality — this reveals how well you understand Java's memory model at a fundamental level.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying '== compares values and .equals() compares objects' — it's the opposite. Or forgetting about the String pool optimization.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the String pool, why "hello" == "hello" is true (interning), and mention that you should override both equals() and hashCode() together.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`==` compares references, `.equals()` compares content** — `==` checks if two variables point to the same memory address; `.equals()` checks meaningful value equality
- **String pool makes `==` deceptive** — `"hello" == "hello"` is true because literals share a pooled reference, but `new String("hello") == new String("hello")` is false
- **Override `equals()` and `hashCode()` together** — HashMap and HashSet rely on the contract that equal objects must have the same hash code
- **`Objects.equals(a, b)` is null-safe** — prevents NullPointerException when either argument could be null
- **Integer cache trap** — `==` works for Integer values -128 to 127 (cached) but fails for larger values; always use `.equals()` for wrapper types

This is about reference equality versus value equality, and it's one of the most common sources of bugs for Java beginners.

**== (double equals)** checks if two references point to the **same object in memory**. It compares memory addresses, not content. For primitives like `int`, `char`, `boolean`, this works fine because primitives are stored by value — `5 == 5` is true.

But for objects, == asks: 'Are these literally the same object?' Not 'Do they contain the same data?'

**`.equals()`** checks if two objects are **meaningfully equal** — do they represent the same value? The `String` class overrides `.equals()` to compare character-by-character. So `"hello".equals("hello")` returns true even if they're different String objects.

Here's the trap that catches almost everyone once:

Say you assign `new String("hello")` to two variables: `==` is false because those are two different objects on the heap, while `.equals` is true because the character sequence is the same.

But wait — `"hello" == "hello"` is actually **true**. Why? Because Java has a **String pool**. When you write a string literal, Java checks the pool first. If `"hello"` already exists, it reuses the same reference. So both variables point to the same pooled String object.

## Java's Memory Model: Why This Question Exists

The `==` vs `.equals()` confusion exists because of how Java stores objects in memory. Understanding the **stack** and **heap** makes the behavior intuitive instead of magical.

### Stack vs Heap

Primitives (`int`, `boolean`, `char`, `double`) live on the **stack** — they store the actual value directly. When you write `int x = 5`, the stack holds the number 5. `==` compares these values directly, which is why `5 == 5` works as expected.

Objects live on the **heap**. A variable like `String name` doesn't hold the string itself — it holds a **reference** (memory address) pointing to the String object on the heap. When you write `==` for objects, you're comparing these addresses, not the content they point to.

```java
// Two references, two different heap objects
String a = new String("hello");  // heap address: 0x1A2B
String b = new String("hello");  // heap address: 0x3C4D
System.out.println(a == b);       // false: 0x1A2B != 0x3C4D
System.out.println(a.equals(b));  // true: both contain "hello"
```

### The String Pool: Why Literals Behave Differently

Java maintains a **String pool** (also called the intern pool) in a special area of heap memory. When you write a string literal like `"hello"`, Java checks the pool first. If `"hello"` already exists there, it returns the same reference. This is an optimization — strings are immutable, so sharing is safe.

```java
String s1 = "hello";   // goes to pool, gets reference 0xABCD
String s2 = "hello";   // pool lookup: "hello" exists, reuse 0xABCD
System.out.println(s1 == s2);  // true: same pooled reference

String s3 = new String("hello");  // forced new heap object, 0xEF01
System.out.println(s1 == s3);     // false: pool ref vs heap ref
System.out.println(s1 == s3.intern());  // true: intern() returns pool ref
```

The `intern()` method manually adds a string to the pool and returns the canonical reference. But relying on `==` for string comparison is a code smell — always use `.equals()` regardless of how the string was created.

### The equals/hashCode Contract

When you override `equals()` in your own classes, you **must** also override `hashCode()`. This is not just a best practice — it's a requirement of the Java specification. `HashMap`, `HashSet`, and `Hashtable` depend on this contract:

**Rule**: If `a.equals(b)` is `true`, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must also be `true`. The reverse is not required — unequal objects may share a hash code (collision).

```java
// What happens without hashCode override:
Map<Employee, String> map = new HashMap<>();
Employee emp1 = new Employee(1, "Alice");
map.put(emp1, "Engineering");

Employee emp2 = new Employee(1, "Alice");  // same data
System.out.println(emp1.equals(emp2));     // true (equals overridden)
System.out.println(map.get(emp2));          // null! wrong hash bucket

// HashMap flow: hashCode(emp2) → bucket X
// But emp1 is in bucket Y (different default hashCode)
// The key is never found
```

### The Integer Cache Trap

Java caches `Integer` objects from -128 to 127 in `IntegerCache`. Autoboxing within this range returns the cached instance, so `==` works accidentally. Outside this range, new objects are created:

```java
Integer a = 127;   // cached
Integer b = 127;   // same cached object
a == b;            // true (same reference)

Integer c = 128;   // new object (outside cache)
Integer d = 128;   // another new object
c == d;            // false (different references)
c.equals(d);       // true (same value)
```

This trap extends to all wrapper types — `Long`, `Short`, `Byte` have similar caches. The rule is simple: **always use `.equals()` for wrapper types**.

- Always use .equals() for String comparison — using == is the #1 beginner bug in Java
- If you override equals(), you MUST override hashCode() — HashMap/HashSet rely on this contract
- The String pool (intern pool) means literal strings reuse references — but never rely on this behavior in production code
- For wrapper classes (Integer, Double), == works for small cached values (-128 to 127 for Integer) but fails for larger values — another trap
- Objects.equals(a, b) is null-safe — use it when either argument could be null

Create a `Student` class with `id` and `name` fields. Override equals() and hashCode() so that two Student objects with the same id are considered equal. Then prove it works by adding Students to a HashSet.

questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList in Java? When would you choose one over the other?
questions.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList in Java
questions.direct_answer: ArrayList uses a dynamic array internally — fast random access (O(1) get by index), but slow insertions/deletions in the middle (O(n) because elements must shift). LinkedList uses doubly-linked nodes — fast insertions/deletions at head/tail (O(1)), but slow random access (O(n) because you must traverse). In practice, ArrayList wins for 95% of use cases because CPU cache locality makes array-based structures much faster than pointer-chasing in linked lists.

interviewer_intent.testing: Do you understand time complexity trade-offs and, more importantly, can you justify a choice based on actual access patterns — not just theory?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'LinkedList is better for insertions' without mentioning that finding the insertion point is O(n) too — so total time is often worse than ArrayList.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention CPU cache locality and why ArrayList is almost always faster in practice despite theoretical advantages of LinkedList. Show you think beyond Big-O.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **ArrayList for 95% of use cases** — O(1) random access, contiguous memory layout gives 10-100x faster iteration due to CPU cache locality
- **LinkedList wastes memory** — each node stores data + two pointers, using ~3x more memory than ArrayList per element
- **LinkedList's insert advantage is theoretical** — finding the insertion point is O(n), so total time is often worse than ArrayList's O(n) shift
- **Use ArrayDeque, not LinkedList** — for queue/stack behavior, ArrayDeque is faster and uses less memory than LinkedList
- **ArrayList grows by 1.5x** — `add()` is amortized O(1); pre-size with `new ArrayList<>(expectedSize)` to avoid repeated resizing

Think of ArrayList as a row of numbered lockers in a hallway. You can go directly to locker #47 without passing any others — that's O(1) random access. But if you want to insert a new locker in the middle, every locker after it has to shift down one position.

LinkedList is like a chain of treasure hunt clues. Each clue tells you where the next one is. Adding a new clue between two existing ones is easy — just update two pointers. But to find clue #47, you have to start at the beginning and follow the chain one by one.

**When to use ArrayList (almost always):**
- You access elements by index frequently
- You mostly add/remove at the end of the list
- You iterate through the list (sequential access is blazing fast due to cache locality)

**When LinkedList might win:**
- You constantly add/remove at the beginning of the list (ArrayList shifts everything)
- You're using it as a Queue or Deque (LinkedList implements both interfaces)
- Your list is used more as a buffer with frequent head/tail operations

Honest truth: Java's own `ArrayList` documentation essentially recommends it as the default choice. LinkedList's theoretical O(1) insert advantage rarely matters in practice because modern CPUs are optimized for contiguous memory (arrays), not pointer-chasing (linked nodes scattered across memory).

- ArrayList's get(index) is O(1), LinkedList's is O(n) — this alone makes ArrayList the default for most cases
- ArrayList.add(element) is amortized O(1) — it only resizes when capacity is exceeded (1.5x growth factor)
- LinkedList uses ~3x more memory than ArrayList per element (each node stores data + prev pointer + next pointer)
- CPU cache locality: ArrayList elements sit next to each other in memory, LinkedList nodes are scattered — this makes ArrayList 10-100x faster for iteration
- Use ArrayDeque instead of LinkedList for queue/stack behavior — it's faster and uses less memory
